items.title: Understanding by interpreter mode is barely measured
items.whyItMatters: The investment choice between in-person and video depends on it, yet only three small studies measured it and none tested equivalence (claim c2).
items.opportunity: State this gap plainly to the committee and recommend local measurement of understanding by mode.

items.title: Overlap and low review quality
items.whyItMatters: Most reviews are critically low in confidence and share primary studies (claim c3), so counting reviews overstates agreement.
items.opportunity: Rate each review with a validated tool and compute overlap before synthesis.

items.title: The locally cited landmark trial cannot be traced
items.whyItMatters: A model lead presents it as a landmark with an identifier that no retrieval or check supports; citing it would mislead the committee.
items.opportunity: Keep it out of the evidence base unless an identity check finds it.

items.title: Languages and groups missing from the evidence
items.whyItMatters: Reviews concentrate on a few widely spoken languages; patients of rare languages, deaf patients using signed languages and older patients relying on family are less represented.
items.opportunity: Chart the languages and populations covered by each review.

items.title: Patient-reported understanding as the core outcome
items.whyItMatters: Satisfaction and clinician-reported delivery dominate (claim c4).
items.opportunity: Make patient-reported understanding the primary outcome of the overview.

errorsFound: The belief that video interpreting is proven equivalent to in-person for understanding rests on an untraceable study; the retrieved reviews do not support it.
reevaluation: The gaps confirm an umbrella review that rates quality, handles overlap and reports the video question as open.
summary: Five gaps; the unmeasured outcome by mode and review overlap and quality are high severity.
